11711-when-hearts-are-trumps:
Tom Hall's When Hearts are Trumps, sixth edition dated September 1898, gathers verses first printed in Life, Truth, Town Topics, Vogue, and Munsey's Magazine over five years. Hall thanks those editors for leave to reprint the majority.

Contents run from kings, queens, and bowers through the perfect face, a moonlight sonata, and a kiss, to a problem to Phyllis and reading a letter. One poem tells of taking little Meg to a ball for two dollars, in calico for satin and broadcloth of blue jeans, yet grand as a queen. The book is light society verse of the 1890s, witty and sentimental by turns.
12938-the-brighton-boys-with-the-flying-:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll's Brighton Boys with the Flying Corps follows Jimmy Hill and his Brighton Academy friends into wartime aviation. Headlines declaring the war will be won in the air greet Jimmy at breakfast. A French lad named Louis Deschamps, whose father serves as a colonel of Zouaves, joins the school story. Training, air fights, and a raid on Essen follow.

A farewell scene shows Joe telling his mother that going feels bigger than fate, almost holy, while she answers that such boys could not stay home. Driscoll writes with warm patriotism and flying detail. The book offers boys' air-war adventure from the First World War years.
13151-the-christian-life-its-course-its-:
Thomas Arnold, head master of Rugby, published The Christian Life in a fifth London edition in 1856, gathering sermons on faith's course, hindrances, and helps. Arnold opens by parting from Archbishop Laud's followers: he backs the church as a living power, but not when church means clergy and hierarchy alone. That point, he says, was the first great apostasy.

Later sermons urge Christians not to glory in party, since Paul, Apollos, and Peter are all theirs, but they are Christ's. Arnold also treats the empty tomb, where John and Peter believed though they had not yet seen the risen Jesus. The sermons are earnest, plain, and broad, written by a schoolmaster who shaped Victorian ideas of character.
14739-the-altar-steps:
Compton Mackenzie's The Altar Steps, published by George H. Doran in New York in 1922, is the prelude to The Parson's Progress. Mackenzie inscribes it with deepest affection to his mother, and notes that the only portrait in the book is of one now dead.

The contents trace a young man's road toward the priesthood: the bishop's shadow, the Lima Street mission, religious education, life at Nancepean, a wreck, Slowbridge, Whit-Sunday, and the Silchester College mission. Later chapters reach Malford Abbey and the Order of St. George. A guardian's letter hands a nephew over to a vicar's care. The novel is a rich picture of Anglican devotion.
15155-windjammers-and-sea-tramps:
Walter Runciman, a senior seaman and author, gathers sea experiences and opinions in this second edition of 1905, dedicated to friends in the shipping world. He opens far back, with a Bristol merchant jailed by Spain's Holy Office and the revenge that followed, then moves toward Britain's rise at sea. Manning the service gets a full chapter.

Runciman writes with a sailor's bluntness about ships, crews, owners, and the change from sail to steam. His stories mix history, gossip, and hard-won judgment. Readers who love the sea will enjoy his voice, even where his views are those of an Edwardian shipman rather than a modern historian.
15498-trumps:
George William Curtis published this novel in 1861, after Nile Notes of a Howadji and Prue and I. Its long contents list moves from school begins and Hope Wayne. It passes a verdict and sentence, society, a New York merchant, and a campaign. Later come a statesman and stateswoman, a portrait and miniature, and Delmonico's. The range signals a broad novel of American life.

Chapters on girls and flowers, old friends and new, dog days, and Aunt Martha give the book its domestic core. Dry goods on commission, fine arts, and a queen and huntress widen it to business and society. Curtis writes with the polish of a New York man of letters, satirizing merchants, artists, and politicians in turn. Trumps reads as a mid-century American social novel, ambitious in scope and fond of its own wit.
16878-observations-upon-the-prophecies-o:
Sir Isaac Newton wrote these observations on the prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John, in two parts, printed in London in 1733 by Darby and Browne and sold by many booksellers. Newton dedicates the sheets to Peter, Lord King, baron of Ockham and Lord High Chancellor, a long friend who, like Newton, made religion his voluntary study amid other work.

Newton reads Daniel and Revelation as coded history, matching beasts, horns, and seals to kingdoms and ages with his usual close reasoning. The book shows the great scientist as a biblical scholar, earnest and systematic. Readers who want Newton beyond physics will find a fascinating, dense work of prophecy, best read with a Bible and a history at hand.
17300-the-story-of-baden-powell-the-wolf:
Harold Begbie published this life of Robert Baden-Powell in London in 1900, the year its hero's fame was at its height. The subtitle, The Wolf that never Sleeps, borrows a name given to Baden-Powell for his watchfulness. Chapters follow his family, home life and holidays, school days at Charterhouse, and service as a dashing hussar, hunter, and scout.

Later chapters cover his regimental life, road making, fire fighting, and work in rags and tatters among ordinary soldiers. Begbie writes in an admiring tone, presenting Baden-Powell as a model for English youth. Readers get a brisk, hero-centred biography from the very moment its subject became a public figure, useful for the myth as much as the man.
17559-on-the-church-steps:
Sarah C. Hallowell wrote this novel, compiled from sections published in Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science from August to October 1873. The first chapter opens with the narrator admiring Bessie as she sits on the church steps, a strange resting place. Behind them lie the Woolsey woods, with pine fragrance and soft rushes of scented air, and lakes lie calm in the distance.

Readers get a gentle American romance of the 1870s, told in a reflective, picturesque voice. The church steps of the title give the book its meeting place and its mood. The novel suits readers of periodical fiction and of quiet domestic romance.
18432-fowler-s-household-helps-over-300-:
A. L. Fowler compiled over three hundred useful and valuable helps about the home, published at Albany in 1916 by the Household Publishing Company. Fowler dedicates the book to the efficient, up-to-date housekeepers of the land, hoping to increase their efficiency further. The author does not guarantee every help, but says they were carefully compiled from reliable sources and should work if directions are followed.

The book opens with the care and use of gas appliances and gas ranges. Clean tops, ovens, and drip pans often. Clean the broiler every time, and clear clogged burner holes with wire or a hairpin. A complete index makes each help easy to find. Readers get a housekeeper's handbook in pocket form: short, practical notes for running a home well, cheaply, and without waste.
18612-from-the-housetops:
George Barr McCutcheon published this novel at New York in 1916 with Dodd, Mead and Company, with pictures by F. Graham Cootes. It opens in 1912 with Templeton Thorpe, seventy-seven and worth many millions, about to marry for the second time a girl of twenty-two, as he had in 1860. His grandson Braden, twenty-nine, storms in to protest the match to Mrs. Tresslyn.

Thirty chapters follow the clash over wealth, marriage, and family duty, with McCutcheon's usual wit and romance. The title points to secrets aired in public and fortunes fought over in the open. Readers of popular society fiction will find a brisk, entertaining tale.
21705-in-the-track-of-the-troops:
War in Europe gives R. M. Ballantyne the setting for this tale of a young man swept along behind an army. The narrator tells his own story, starting with his boyhood love of taking things apart to see how they worked. That habit of pulling the world to pieces shapes the teller of the tale. He writes with pride, humor, and a strong wish to seem wise.

What follows is a string of personal adventures in the path of marching troops. Ballantyne mixes real scenes of modern war with the narrator's mishaps and narrow escapes. The result is part war report and part comic confession, told in a voice that keeps undercutting its own grand claims.
21749-man-on-the-ocean-a-book-about-boat:
Ships themselves are the subject of this Ballantyne book, which calls a great ship one of the most wonderful things men have made. A ship, he says, is a wooden house built to float, a small moving hotel on the sea. It carries its own little country of people across trackless water for months at a time.

The chapters walk through boats and ships of many kinds and ages. Ballantyne explains how they are built, rigged, sailed, and handled in storms. He wrote it for readers who loved his sea tales and wanted the facts behind them. It is a plain-spoken tour of man's oldest great machine, told by a man who never tired of the sea.
21976-three-years-in-the-sixth-corps:
The Sixth Corps of the Army of the Potomac gets its chronicle in George T. Stevens's Three Years in the Sixth Corps, published at Albany in 1866. Stevens served as surgeon of the 77th New York Volunteers. He offers the book to his old comrades, hoping it recalls their varied experiences in an unparalleled body of men. General John Sedgwick, the corps' beloved commander, fronts the volume.

Stevens wrote mostly from notes taken amid the scenes themselves, with official reports and officers' letters in support. Marches, battles, camps, and hospital scenes pass in order from 1861 to April 1865. He promises no exaggeration and asks brave men's leniency for faults. As a unit history by a man who marched with it, the book keeps a surgeon's eye and a soldier's loyalty.
24149-the-ambulance-made-two-trips:
Murray Leinster wrote this crime story for Astounding Science Fiction in April 1960, with pictures by Schoenherr. Detective Sergeant Fitzgerald finds a fine meerschaum pipe left at his door with no card, a gift he has longed to own. Like other such gifts, he takes it to the orphanage, where the head admits such presents to police have dropped off of late.

Fitzgerald blames Big Jake Connors, a racketeer newly in town with bright ideas, whose largesse is softening the whole force. A lieutenant's wife got a mink stole, and another sergeant got new white-wall tires. Leinster turns the old trick of setting a thief to catch a thief. Readers get a brisk tale of bribes, pride, and one honest cop.
24516-the-crystal-hunters-a-boy-s-advent:
George Manville Fenn wrote this boys' adventure of crystal hunting in the higher Alps. A party of English people travels to the Swiss mountains, not only for scenery but for crystals found in caves near the tops of glaciers. A guide promises to be discreet about their doings, but someone else is on the mountain, watching what they find.

Fenn's tale brings crevasses, avalanches, ice-falls, and tumbling rocks, with a thief making off with hard-won specimens. The ending holds a surprise. Young readers get a tense, old-fashioned mountain adventure, full of danger, snow, and the thrill of a rare find.
24606-history-of-the-nineteenth-army-cor:
Richard B. Irwin wrote this history of the Nineteenth Army Corps, the Union corps that fought in Louisiana, the Red River campaign, and the Shenandoah Valley. Irwin's chapters follow the corps from its organisation through battles, marches, and sieges, with notes on losses in battle and on the officers who led it.

Later chapters include the dam on the Red River, Fisher's Hill, and the fighting in the Valley, with footnotes gathered at the end of each chapter. Irwin writes as a soldier-historian, careful with detail and loyal to his corps. Readers of Civil War history will find this a solid regimental history of a hard-fought command.
25007-fifty-soups:
Thomas J. Murrey's Fifty Soups, in its eighth edition from Frederick A. Stokes, gathers the working knowledge of a professional caterer of Philadelphia's Continental Hotel and New York's Astor House. Remarks on soups open the book. Artichoke, asparagus, barley, bean purée, beef stock and beef tea, bouille-abaisse, cauliflower, celery cream, chestnut, chicken broth and soup, clam broth and chowder, consommé, and crab bisque follow. The list runs the full kitchen range.

Murrey favors economy without meanness: giblet soup, made from the legs, neck, heart, wings, and gizzard of poultry, turns holiday odds and ends to account with a little rice. Water or a share of the soup itself provides the cooking liquid for the dumplings before serving. Green turtle soup, he notes, is less expensive and difficult than housewives imagine, though the canned sort is not always made from turtle. The book is a practical classic.
25768-tartarin-on-the-alps:
Alphonse Daudet writes Tartarin on the Alps. It opens on 10 August 1880 at the Rigi-Kulm. A yellow fog with snow spirals wraps the summit hotel. The hotel stands glassed like a conservatory and massive as a citadel. Tourists, worshippers of the sun, alight for a night and a day.

Around a table of six hundred covers, with rice and prunes and an improvised ball, an unknown signs the hotel register P. C. A. Tartarin, Daudet's boastful Provencal hero, climbs into Alpine comedy, as guidebook sunsets, frozen chambers, and reading room divans frame a satire on tourism and tall tales.
2689-over-the-teacups:
Oliver W. Holmes wrote this late series of papers over the teacups, pleased by a kind reception greater than he had dared to hope. A late comer among ardent candidates for public attention, he feared he had already had his day, like the Frenchman told he had come again.

The papers that follow chat about age, books, science, and Boston life, with the Doctor's familiar wit. Holmes writes as an old friend at the table, not a lecturer. The book charms as a farewell performance, gentle, learned, and full of the humor of a long life.
28493-baby-nightcaps:
Baby Nightcaps, entered in 1859 by Fanny Barrow and published by D. Appleton of New York in 1860, comes from the author of Nightcaps and Aunt Fanny's Stories. It opens with a nightcap letter from Aunt Fanny to a dear little darling, continuing a form lame Charley named in the earlier book. The stories are meant to be read at bedtime, one by one.

Contents include a story told to Minnie, Lillie's sayings and doings showing the effects of a good example, and Jack and his friends. Little Helen follows, with the tale of how little Susie was lost and found. Young readers get gentle lessons in kindness, care, and good conduct, wrapped in short tales.
28802-the-fairy-nightcaps:
Fanny Barrow, writing as Aunt Fanny, wrote this 1861 book, the sixth and last of her Nightcap books for children. Dedicated to Massa Charles, it gathers fairy life in a beautiful hollow below Crow Nest Mountain. A children's journey to West Point, a midsummer ball, Idlewild, a stag dance, and a battle of the fairies follow. A closing chapter tells the death of Charley.

Aunt Fanny tells her young readers that one story was altered from a clever grown folks' book nearly two hundred years old, but she swears all the rest is true. Her preface asks only that children keep one kind thought of her warm in their hearts. Readers get a gentle, old-fashioned fairy book, written with love and meant to be read at bedtime.
29111-what-the-blackbird-said-a-story-in:
Mrs. Frederick Locker wrote this children's story in four chirps, published in London in 1881 with illustrations by Randolph Caldecott. Each chirp is a season: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. The tale follows a fine young blackbird through a dreary winter, perched on a bare limb of a wide lime tree.

Around him gather his friends, a robin and a rook, and the three birds share the year's turns together. Locker dedicated the book to her children Godfrey and Dorothy. Readers get a gentle Victorian animal story, beautifully illustrated, about friendship and the seasons told through birds.
31269-upon-the-tree-tops:
Olive Thorne Miller's 1897 bird book, published by Houghton, Mifflin with illustrations by J. Carter Beard, gathers thirteen studies of birds in the treetops. Chapters follow tramps with an enthusiast, a mysterious stranger, a thorn-tree nest, the witching wren, whimsical ways in bird-land, and the bird of the musical wing. They go on to a lady in green, young America in feathers, a meadow walk, a Colorado nook, the idyl of an empty lot, the solitaire, and incompatibility in the oriole family.

Miller began with a bird-room for close observation and found her feathered neighbors as individual in character as people. She credits her daughter Mary Mann Miller for the facts of two chapters and Frederic A. Ober for notes on a solitaire. The book is a classic of patient, affectionate American bird study.
33098-ancient-and-modern-ships-part-1-wo:
Sir George C. V. Holmes's Ancient and Modern Ships, Part One: Wooden Sailing-Ships, surveys sailing ships with seventy-four illustrations. It was issued by the Victoria and Albert Museum as a science handbook in a revised edition of 1906. Holmes writes for museum visitors and students who want to understand how wooden ships were built, rigged, and sailed, from ancient craft to the great sailing ships of recent times. He was formerly secretary of the Institution of Naval Architects.

Priced at one shilling and sixpence in paper wrapper, the handbook was meant to be carried and used, not shelved as a showpiece. Its pictures and clear text explain hulls, sails, and gear in terms a general reader can follow. For maritime historians and model makers, it remains a handy, authoritative introduction to the age of sail, produced by a museum that knew its ships from the inside.
33767-campward-ho-a-manual-for-girl-scou:
Girl Scouts Incorporated published this 1920 manual for organizing and directing large, self-supporting camps for girls, from national headquarters at 189 Lexington Avenue, New York. Opening with Chaucer on April pilgrimages, the book sets out the Scout motto, Be Prepared, the slogan, and Do a Good Turn Daily. The book also sets out the promise to do duty to God and country, help others, and obey the Scout Laws. The book also sets out ten laws from trustworthy honor to cleanliness in thought, word, and deed.

Chapters on planning, equipment, health, program, and campcraft cover the needs of those undertaking camps at scale. The manual reflects the early Girl Scout movement's blend of outdoor life, service, and character training, aimed at leaders rather than campers alone. Historians of youth organizations and camping will find a detailed picture of how large girls' camps were run a century ago.
33868-the-casque-s-lark-or-victoria-the-:
Eugene Sue wrote this volume as part of his vast Mysteries of the People, a history of a working family across the ages. The Casque's Lark, or Victoria, the Mother of the Camps, follows Victoria, a woman of the camps, through war and hardship. It stands among companion volumes on the gold sickle, the brass bell, the iron collar, and the silver cross.

Sue uses one family's fortunes to tell the long story of common people in France. Victoria's strength and care for her people give the volume its heart. The book offers a dramatic, populist chapter in Sue's great serial history.
34161-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this seventh volume of The Story of the Great War, published in New York in 1919 by P. F. Collier and Son, with Allen L. Churchill as associate editor and Francis Trevelyan Miller as editor in chief. Prefaces cover what the war means to America, naval lessons, the world's war, theatres of campaigns, and the war correspondent.

The volume treats American food and ships, Palestine, Italy invaded, the great German offensive, Americans in Picardy and on the Marne, and Foch's counteroffensive. Part One follows the Western Front through Ypres, Lens, Verdun, and Haig's strikes. The book offers a full, illustrated record of the war's later year.
34446-cottontail-rabbits-in-relation-to-:
Lantz, an assistant biologist, wrote this Farmers' Bulletin number 702 for the Department of Agriculture, issued January 17, 1916. Its subject is cottontail rabbits in relation to trees and farm crops. Among the serious pests in orchards and tree plantations, the introduction says, are the several native species of rabbits. They damage garden truck and other crops too, above all on lands newly opened to farming.

The bulletin treats the rabbits' habits, their protection, and the means of holding them down: natural enemies, hunting, trapping, poisoning, and disease. Then it turns to defense: rabbit-proof fences, tree guards, washes, and devices. It balances the farmer's war with a word for the rabbit's place. Such bulletins were Washington's free advice to every orchardist, and this one is thorough and humane.
3462-more-hunting-wasps:
Jean Henri Fabre completes his wasp essays in this volume, the third part of his collected work on wasps after The Hunting Wasps and the Mason Wasps. Fourteen chapters cover the Ammophila, the Bembex, and other hunting wasps, following how each kind captures prey, digs a nest, and stocks it for its young. Notes point readers back to earlier chapters for fuller accounts.

Fabre's method is patient watching in the field, not laboratory theory. He records the wasp's sting, its choice of caterpillar, and its care for eggs it will never see hatch. The book suits readers who enjoy natural history written with clarity and wonder, and it closes a set that made Fabre famous among insect lovers.
35213-afloat-in-the-forest-or-a-voyage-a:
Afloat in the Forest, or a Voyage among the Tree Tops, is an adventure tale by Captain Mayne Reid. The Boston edition is dated eighteen sixty seven. Chapter one is called The Brothers at Home. It opens in Cornwall, not twenty miles from Land's End, twenty years before the tale's present.

A Cornish gentleman named Trevannion has lately died there, the chapter says. He kept open house so freely that the family estate was lost within months of his death. His two sons, Ralph and Richard, are left landless and houseless. A thousand pounds apiece is all that remains to them. Folk whispered that even that came from the solicitor who managed their father's affairs. That lawyer now owns the property himself, the tale hints.
36064-farm-gardening-with-hints-on-cheap:
Johnson and Stokes, seed growers of Philadelphia, compiled this guide to farm gardening in 1898. A picture of hilling celery, as market gardeners near that city practice it, stands at the front. The preface speaks plainly about money.

Farmers east of the Mississippi, the firm argues, can no longer grow grain or fatten cattle against western competition. Dairying pays, but cash crops near rail lines pay better. The book promises vegetables that beat grain, with hints on growing them. First comes making the soil rich, then choice of location. Chapters sort vegetables for farm culture everywhere and in some places only, then treat sashes, bedding plants, and the strawberry.
36249-among-the-canadian-alps:
Among the Canadian Alps is a mountain travel book by Lawrence Burpee, printed at New York by the John Lane Company in 1914. Burpee was a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. The book holds four illustrations in colour, forty-five reproductions from photographs, and five maps. The frontispiece shows Berg Lake and Tumbling Glacier. Burpee dated his preface from Ottawa in October 1914.

Fourteen chapters tour the ranges. They begin with the lure of the mountains and the national parks of Canada. Then come Banff, the Canadian Matterhorn, Lake Louise, and the valley of the Yoho. The Illecillewaet glacier and the caves of Nakimu follow. Two chapters treat mountain climbing and climbers, and climbing in the Selkirks. Jasper and the Moose River trail close the journey, with the Monarch of the Rockies between them. A bibliography ends the book.
36943-twenty-quick-soups:
Twenty Quick Soups is a cook book by Mrs Rorer, the Philadelphia cooking teacher. Arnold and Company published it at Philadelphia in 1894. It was one of six small volumes at twenty five cents each. Fifteen New Ways for Oysters and How to Use a Chafing Dish were its mates. Colonial Recipes, Sandwiches, and Dainties completed that little set. Each volume was bound in a different coloured linen cloth. The contents list the soups by their chief ingredient. Cream of Asparagus opens the recipes.

Cream of Corn, Cream of Lettuce, and Cream of Beets follow. Tomato Soup and Clear Tomato with Sago come next in the list. Brown Broth and Cheese Balls stand midway through the contents. Bisque of Clam and Club Clam Soup serve seafood tastes. Mock Oyster Soup and Cucumber Tapioca Soup close the named list. Rorer's larger cook book ran to nearly six hundred pages.
38359-peeps-at-postage-stamps:
Stanley C Johnson wrote a guide to postage stamps in the Peeps series, published in London in 1915 with sixteen plates holding one hundred sixty three specimen stamps. Portraits of King George the Fifth form the frontispiece. Because of revenue rules, the pictures are printed in black rather than color. An introduction explains the plan.

Chapters explain philatelic terms and how to form a collection. Specializing, the stamps of Great Britain, and stamps worth fortunes follow. Common stamps, forged stamps, and pioneers of postage each get a chapter. Commemorative and war stamps close the main text. Johnson wrote for young collectors and general readers alike.
39542-the-alps:
Alps is a descriptive book written by W Martin Conway and painted by A D McCormick. The London edition is dated nineteen oh four. A front picture shows haymakers in the Val Maggia carrying enormous loads. Contents run to twelve chapters. They open with the treasures of the snow and how to see mountains.

How mountains are made and all sorts and conditions of Alps follow. The moods of the mountains and mountains all the year round take their turns. Types of alpine peaks, passes, and glaciers earn chapters of their own. Alpine pastures and the human interest come near the end. A chapter on volcanoes closes the list. The picture list runs to views of Bern, the Jungfrau, and the lakes. Loads carried by women haymakers, one caption says, can top twice the woman's height.
40504-ginger-snaps:
Ginger-Snaps is a book of short comic sketches by Fanny Fern, published at New York in 1870. Fern had won her name with Fern Leaves and like books. Her preface tells how, as a girl, she played at making ginger-snaps. She tossed in all the ginger in the spice box, more or less. If these pieces bite, she says, blame the habit of her youth. They are not a square meal, she warns. They are to be nibbled at on a steamboat or a train, or under country trees.

The contents list brief takes on the life of her day. Dinner parties, a bride's new house, and literary aspirants all get a piece. Why wear mourning, female clerks, and the woman's millennium stand in the run. A sermon to Plymouth pulpit and a trip to Richmond fill other pages.
41712-connie-morgan-in-the-lumber-camps:
James Hendryx sent his boy hero Connie Morgan south from Alaska to the logging woods in a tale of 1919. Putnam published it in New York and London. The first scene shows Connie's partner, Waseche Bill, in a rage at a costly dictionary. The book, he says, is full of words no one uses and lacks the plain ones a man needs.

Bill wants to write to Mike Gillum, a man known all along the Tanana and in the woods outside. Connie, who learned spelling at school, is pressed to help. The chapters ahead bring a bear cat tamed, a new camp laid out, and the IWW showing its hand. A log drive, a masked rogue named Slue Foot Magee, and a last delivery close the tale. It is brisk north woods fun for boys.
41737-burton-of-the-flying-corps:
Herbert Strang wrote Burton of the Flying Corps, a boys' war story first printed in London in 1916. Brock drew its pictures, including color plates. The contents list promises five tales, each with a short note on what Burton does in it.

In the first, Burton travels to Ostend in pursuit of a spy. In others he faces a death's head hussar in a French chateau, catches a German agent in Bulgaria, and suffers an accident in Macedonia. The last tale turns to trench warfare in Flanders and a missing platoon. Strang wrote many such books for boys during the war, mixing flight, spies, and pluck in short, self contained adventures.
42604-stories-of-the-ships:
Stories of the Ships is a naval war book by Lewis Freeman, a lieutenant who served as official press representative with the Grand Fleet. It was issued at London in 1919 and dedicated to a captain named Ellerton. The first part tells the stories of two ships in turn. One runs from Plymouth to the Falklands and into battle there.

The second ship's story is told first as a signalman's tale, then as an account of naval brutality by the enemy. A middle part turns to life in the fleet: a battleship at sea, a North Sea sweep, and a visit to the fleet. Health and economy in the fleet get their own chapters. Christmas in a happy ship and the work of the stokers close that part, before a last part on America's arrival.
43876-california-athabascan-groups:
Martin A Baumhoff wrote California Athabascan Groups for the Anthropological Records of the University of California. The study came out at Berkeley in August nineteen hundred fifty eight. It runs from page one hundred fifty seven to two hundred thirty eight. Eighteen maps and three plates go with the text.

Baumhoff first maps where each group’s land began and ended. He then treats the Kato, Wailaki, Lassik, and Sinkyone in turn. The Mattole, Bear River, Whilkut, and Hupa close the list. Fish counts help him guess how many folk once lived there. Notes from C Hart Merriam fill one add-on part. A L Kroeber adds notes on the upper Eel River folk. Scholars of Native California will find town sites pinned down here.
44348-dastral-of-the-flying-corps:
Rowland Walker wrote Dastral of the Flying Corps, a boys' tale of the air war first published in 1917 and reprinted. It stands in the Great Adventure Series, with tales by Percy Westerman and others, and is issued by Partridge of London. Walker gave the book to the pilots, observers, and air-mechanics of the Royal Flying Corps. The plate shows a blazing mass falling thousands of feet.

The eleven chapters run from Dastral winning his pilot's badge through the ferry pilot and over the German lines. A bombing raid, a Zeppelin night, and the raid on Krupps follow, to Himmelman's last fight and a Blighty wound. The tale opens while the German guns thunder at the gates of Verdun. Walker wrote for boys at home while the war raged, and his hero's fights give the Flying Corps a bold face.
4540-in-his-steps:
Charles M. Sheldon sets this Christian novel in an American town church, opening with the Reverend Henry Maxwell struggling to finish his Sunday sermon. Maxwell, his wife Mary, and their congregation are soon faced with a simple, hard question drawn from the Bible: what would Jesus do in their place? The story asks its readers to take that question out of church and into daily work.

Members of the church pledge to act on the question for a year, and their choices touch business, newspapers, charity, art, and family life. Some lose money or standing, while others find a new purpose. Sheldon writes plainly, aiming at conscience rather than fine style. Readers get a moral tale that has shaped church discussion for generations, and a clear picture of its famous challenge in action.
46181-the-forty-third-regiment-united-st:
The Forty-Third Regiment, United States Colored Troops is a regimental history printed by Wible at Gettysburg in 1866, just after the Civil War. Its introduction is signed by Mickley, late chaplain of the regiment. No apology is necessary for the publication, he writes, since its object is neither unworthy nor mercenary. The pages were elicited by request of numerous friends of the officers and of the colored troops.

Their object is not simply to give succinct statements of individual military history. They furnish an unanswerable argument for the colored troops as an element in the service of freedom and the Union. Their extraordinary good discipline, efficiency, and bravery are the brief. A list of the regiment's commissioned officers follows the introduction. A biographical passage preserved in the copy follows the general's early life.
46299-with-the-french-flying-corps:
Carroll Dana Winslow, an American serving with the French Flying Corps, wrote this account of learning to fight in the air. It came out in New York in January 1917, months before America entered the Great War. He gives the book to his father.

Contents trace his path: enlistment, first principles, and learning to fly at the school at Chartres. He passes his final tests, watches a Zeppelin raid over Paris, and wins orders to the front. In the Verdun sector he makes his first flight over the lines and learns to work with the artillery. Readers get the air war at its birth, told by a young volunteer.
46822-souvenir-album-of-the-great-europe:
Souvenir Album of the Great European War is a picture album of the First World War, copyrighted in 1914 by the Osborne Company of Newark, New Jersey. Osborne made art calendars and gave the album to its customers. Its pictures are reproduced from actual photographs taken in Europe. Many had already appeared, in cruder form, in the newspapers.

The introduction argues that photographs of the most stupendous war in history hold worldwide interest and lasting value. Here they are printed in the actual colours of life, in a form worth preserving. The pictures first sold as post cards. A pictorial map of the battlegrounds accompanies the plates.
47209-hours-of-exercise-in-the-alps:
Hours of Exercise in the Alps, by John Tyndall, gathers the great physicist's papers on climbing and glaciers. This authorized edition was published in New York in 1896.

Tyndall says the climbing was often only the peg on which a thousand other exercises hung. The papers, written over ten years, appear in the order of the climbs they describe. Two pieces by other hands are included with leave: one by Vaughan Hawkins tells of the first attack ever made on the Matterhorn. Another, by Philip Gossett, tells of a climb that ended in the death of a famed and beloved guide. Since his Glaciers of the Alps was out of print, Tyndall adds notes on the ice world at the end. A voyage to Oran closes the book.
47714-english-heraldic-book-stamps:
Cyril Davenport wrote this study of English heraldic book-stamps, printed by Archibald Constable of London in 1909. Davenport had written The Book. The frontispiece shows the book-stamp of the King, by his gracious permission, and a note sends the reader to page 155 for its account. A long introduction runs to page 41, and the coats-of-arms fill the body to page 413.

Davenport teaches the metals, colours, and furs of heraldry: ermine with its black tail tips, and vair of blue and white squirrel skins. He warns that tincture lines show on English royal book-stamps only from George the Second's time. Before that, no colour marks the shield, and arms are hard to assign without crests, coronets, and other helps.
48226-dick-donnelly-of-the-paratroops:
Gregory Duncan wrote Dick Donnelly of the Paratroops, printed at Racine with a copyright of 1944, with pictures by Francis Kirn. Whitman's war books for boys put their heroes in every service, and Dick jumps with the paratroops. The chapters run token resistance, a man with two names, and Wadizam Pass, then encircled and break-through.

Plates catch the action: Dick scanning a report of German troop movements, tying a rope around a box, and wishing for a German officer's uniform. By golly, a caption cries, I think we can get away with it. The tale is pure 1944: special missions, not-so-happy landings, and boys doing a man's work behind the lines.
48999-the-boy-scouts-of-the-signal-corps:
Robert Shaler wrote a boys' novel copyrighted in 1914, first in a list of ten Sterling Boy Scout books. Hugh Hardin, leader of the Wolf patrol at seventeen, calls his assistant Billy Worth out of his bunk. Billy's bare foot dangles over a lower bunk, and a boy below tickles it with a wisp of straw. Camp humor opens the tale.

Chapters cover forming the signal corps, a perilous encounter, and a fire in camp. A hike, a sham battle, and a talk around the council fire follow. A mountain adventure closes the contents list. Other titles in the series send scouts to pioneer camp, the life saving crew, and the flying squadron.
49295-after-taps:
George Baker's Globe Drama list fills the volume called After Taps. Walter Baker at Boston sold the plays from 23 Winter Street. Rights in the list were held in 1876 by George Baker himself. He wrote Amateur Dramas, The Mimic Stage, and The Social Stage. Titles in one type are new plays, the key explains to buyers.

Titles in another type are temperance plays in the same key. Dramas in four acts head the list, with casts and prices marked. Better than Gold takes seven men and four women, at twenty-five cents. Our Folks, Enlisted for the War, and My Brother's Keeper stand in three acts. The Little Brown Jug waves the temperance flag in the list. Comediettas follow: a mysterious disappearance and a drop too much among them. The catalogue gives amateur players their repertory in one pamphlet.
50310-mother-goose-for-grown-ups:
Guy Wetmore Carryl rewrites the nursery rhymes as light verse for adults in a book issued by Harper and Brothers in 1900. Peter Newell and Gustave Verbeek drew the pictures. Some pieces first ran in Harper's Magazine and the Saturday Evening Post.

Every title inflates its rhyme into mock-heroic pomp. The Admirable Assertiveness of Jilted Jack leads. The Blatant Brutality of Little Bow Peep follows. Old Mother Hubbard gets a Commendable Castigation. Simple Simon shows Gastronomic Guile. Tom, the Piper's Son shows Inexcusable Improbity. Humpty Dumpty suffers an Opportune Overthrow. Carryl dedicates the book to Constance, across long leagues of sea. His note hopes the rhymes link them in the olden spell. Carryl was a master of the punning ballade. His nonsense verse sparkled in the magazines of the day.
50558-a-tramp-s-scraps:
Tramp Scraps is a book of short pieces by H I M Self, printed in Los Angeles in 1913. Publisher C C Parker of South Broadway issued the tramp writings for the road. A dedication offers the book to anybody, anywhere, anytime in tramp spirit. Contents list scraps named Fire, The Ghost, In a Houseboat, and Animals.

At sea, a quarrel, and other road fragments fill the short table of the volume. Such scraps mix verse, yarn, and travel notes from a life of wandering. The tramp author writes for the casual reader who picks the book up anywhere. American hobo letters of the rail age speak in these loose pages.
51222-a-captive-at-carlsruhe-and-other-g:
Joseph Lee told of his days as a captive in German prison camps. His book came out in London in 1920. Lee wrote his own drawn plates for the book. He had wrote Ballads of Battle and Work-a-Day Warriors. A line at the front jokes that a chamber is prison enough.

Lee gives the book to his fellows in woe from allied lands. Their cheer made long, dull days light, he says. Carlsruhe camp's corner shows in the first plate. Caudry and the road to camp start the tale in part one. Hunger, cold, and hope mark each camp in turn. War readers get a captive's calm, wry voice.
52009-new-lamps:
New Lamps is a science fiction tale by Robert Moore Williams. The text comes from Other Worlds magazine of May 1957 here. Ronson came to the Red Planet on the strangest mission of all. He only knew he wanted to see Les Ro on Mars. He did not know exactly why he sought that strange trader.

Les Ro had the answer to something never answered before, it seems. He traded new lamps for old, the lamps of life itself there. On Mars the dust is yellow and fine beyond all measure. It works into the lung tissues of a human being, causing distress. Jim Ronson sneezes crossing the street toward a dive in the cliff.
52095-dave-dawson-with-the-air-corps:
R Sidney Bowen wrote a war tale of Dave Dawson with the Air Corps. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it from Akron and New York. Rights were held in 1942 by Crown Publishers. Eighteen chapters run from Hangar Flying to Thundering Revenge.

Dave Dawson had flown at Dunkirk, in Libya, and at Singapore in prior books. His friend Freddy Farmer opens the tale on a broad field under a wide sky. Orders, battle plans, lost wings, and Nazi tricks crowd the pages. Boys in war years got fast tales of flight, nerve, and duty in the air.
53431-chats-on-postage-stamps:
Fred Melville wrote Chats on Postage Stamps, one of the Books for Collectors series published in London with frontispieces and many illustrations. The series list shows its fellows: Chats on English China, Old Furniture, Old Prints, Costume, Old Lace and Needlework, Oriental China, Old Miniatures, English Earthenware, Autographs, Pewter, and Old Coins. Most are by Arthur Hayden and a few other hands.

Melville was Britain's great stamp populariser, founder of societies and writer of a shelf of philatelic books. The Chats volumes taught new collectors what to buy, what things were worth, and how to tell the genuine. Stamps were then the commonest collecting craze of all.
54163-ski-runs-in-the-high-alps:
F F Roget wrote Ski-Runs in the High Alps for skiers who climb above the resorts. T Fisher Unwin issued the book in London in nineteen hundred thirteen. Roget held honor posts in two Alpine ski clubs. L M Crisp drew twenty five pictures, and six maps guide the routes.

The first chapter sorts the high snow fields by zone. It warns of glacier risk and the odd warmth found high up in winter. Snow types and storm signs get close study. Guides and porters earn their own notes. Later chapters lay out runs peak by peak. The book suits trained mountaineers more than new skiers. It shows how hard and planned high Alpine ski travel was in its early years.
558-the-thirty-nine-steps:
John Buchan launches Richard Hannay in this brisk spy tale, written during an illness in 1915. Hannay, bored after three months in London, takes in a stranger who dies that night, leaving a notebook of a German plot. Fleeing police and spies, Hannay runs across Scotland by train, road, and moor.

Buchan writes in lean, fast prose, praising the shocker where events march just inside the possible. A literary innkeeper, a radical candidate, and a dry-fly fisherman mark the chase. The novel endures as the model modern thriller, where one man must stop a war plot with wit alone.
56358-the-alps:
The Alps is a survey by Arnold Lunn in the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. Holt issued the American edition; the book was first printed in 1914. Herbert Fisher and Gilbert Murray edited the series. Ten chapters trace man's dealings with the great range. The mediaeval attitude opens the story. The pioneers and the opening up of the Alps follow.

The story of Mont Blanc gets a chapter of its own. Monte Rosa, the Tyrol, and the Oberland come next. The coming of the English marks the age of the clubs. The Matterhorn story forms the book's dark centrepiece. Modern mountaineering and the Alps in literature close the survey. Lunn argues that Rousseau first made mountains fashionable. Before him, men who loved mountains were eccentrics who founded no school.
57761-a-brief-history-of-the-king-s-roya:
A Brief History of the King's Royal Rifle Corps is a regimental history of one of Britain's famed rifle regiments. Its motto, Celer et Audax, swift and bold, heads the book. A long roll of battle honours opens it: Louisburg, Quebec 1759, Martinique, and Havana. Then come the Peninsular names: Roleia, Vimiera, Talavera, Busaco, Fuentes d'Onor, Albuhera, Ciudad Rodrigo, and Badajoz.

Salamanca, Vittoria, the Pyrenees, and Toulouse follow, then the Punjaub, Delhi, the Taku Forts, and Pekin. Egypt, Chitral, and South Africa bring the roll toward the present, with the defence and relief of Ladysmith. The history's sections begin with the regiment's origin and services in North America from 1755 to 1763. It was born as the Royal American Regiment in the French and Indian War. Later parts follow it through the American war, the Peninsula, and the Victorian campaigns. Such brief histories kept a regiment's memory green.
59941-vinzi-a-story-of-the-swiss-alps:
Vinzi, a story of the Swiss Alps, is a children's novel by Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi. The hosted edition belongs to a series called The Stories All Children Love. Its frontispiece shows Vinzi seated on his threshold with a great many things to think over. The tale opens under a June sun on the green slope above the village of Leuk.

The fresh grass on the heights fills the air with fragrance as far as the eye can see. Spyri's Alpine stories centre on children growing up among mountains, with their seasons, work, and faith. The series list around Vinzi names her other books: Gritli's Children, Dora, Mazli, and Cornelli. Heidi stands among them as the most famous. Vinzi is one of the Swiss tales in which Spyri wrote of village childhood.
60700-a-sketch-of-the-29th-regiment-of-c:
I J Hill (Isaac J. Hill), a soldier of the regiment, wrote this sketch of the 29th Regiment of Connecticut Colored Troops, printed at Baltimore in 1867. The title promises a full account of its formation, of all the battles it passed through, and of its final disbandment.

Hill's preface tells his own story first. Born in Pennsylvania in 1826, he was put out to service in Kentucky at six, where law forbade teaching a colored child. He taught himself to read and write. Called to the ministry in 1852, he rode with the 3rd Pennsylvania Cavalry, then enlisted in the 29th in January 1863. The book is a Black veteran's record of his regiment.
60919-with-axe-and-rope-in-the-new-zeala:
George Edward Mannering wrote With Axe and Rope in the New Zealand Alps, published by Longmans in London in 1891. Mannering belonged to the New Zealand Alpine Club. His book is among the first accounts of climbing in the Southern Alps. A photograph shows his party on the Tasman Glacier, roped and ready, with the author among them.

The early chapters describe the route to the Mount Cook district. Mannering explains the Mueller, Hooker, and Tasman valleys for readers who had never seen them. Then come his attempts on Aorangi, the mountain now called Mount Cook. The first attempt ends in defeat, with the perils of river crossing made plain. A flooded camp opens the second. Mannering writes with a pioneer's care for detail: gear, weather, food, and ice. His book helped found New Zealand mountaineering and still serves as a record of the Alps before huts and guides.
61376-the-historical-geography-of-europe:
Volume two of The Historical Geography of Europe, by Edward Freeman, holds the maps for his history. Longmans printed it in London in 1881. Freeman was an honorary fellow of Trinity College, Oxford. The list of maps runs to more than fifty plates. The first maps show Homeric Greece and the Greek colonies. Greece in the fifth century before Christ follows.

Later maps trace Alexander, his successors, and the growth of Rome. The Roman Empire appears under Augustus, under Trajan, and split into prefectures. Medieval and modern maps track France, Spain, and the south east. A map keyed to the Treaty of Berlin closes the main run. Used with volume one, the atlas lets readers watch borders shift age by age.
61406-hannibal-crosses-the-alps:
Cecil Torr wrote Hannibal Crosses the Alps, a study from Cambridge University Press on the most famous march in ancient war. Hannibal led an army from Spain toward Italy, over high passes, with elephants in train. Which pass he used has been argued for centuries, and Torr takes up the question with a scholar's care.

Torr weighs the old Roman and Greek accounts against the ground itself, pass by pass. He tests snow, rock, and road against each claim in the sources. Students of Rome get a tight, learned case, and general readers get a clear guide to a puzzle that still draws debate among historians and walkers alike.
61830-dick-merriwell-s-assurance-or-in-h: Dick Merriwell Assurance, or In His Brother Footsteps, is one tale in the Merriwell series of stories for young men. The series list at the front names Frank and Dick Merriwell. Its stories, priced at fifteen cents, are billed as tales of athletics. The publisher boasts of half a million followers of the brothers and of the high moral tone of the adventures. Dick, the younger brother, follows Frank path at school and on the field in this number.
62316-citadel-of-lost-ships:
Leigh Brackett wrote Citadel of Lost Ships, a science fiction tale printed in Planet Stories in March 1943. The headnote calls it a gypsy world, built of space flotsam and peopled with the few free races of the solar system. Roy Campbell, outcast prey of the Coalition, entered its depths to seek haven for the Kraylens of Venus. He found only a slave trap from which there was no escape.

Brackett was the queen of the planetary romance, and her lost ships' citadel is a port of wrecks and wanderers in space. Campbell must free the enslaved or die among the hulks. Her prose runs lean, hard, and full of color. Readers get top flight space adventure from a master hand.
62640-the-history-and-romance-of-air-mai:
Emil Bruechig wrote this history of air mail stamps, copyrighted at New York in 1936. His office stood at 522 Fifth Avenue, the title page gives in his dealer's style. The history of the flying machine reaches back to man's earliest written records, he begins at the start.

Greek myth shows an interest in the problem of flight, Bruechig writes at the opening. Roman-age philosophers and medieval alchemists left parchments of their thoughts on flying, he adds. From those dreams to streamlined planes the glamour holds, and the stamps that flew the mail carry the romance into a collector's album page by page.
62881-the-tank-corps:
The Tank Corps, by Clough Williams-Ellis and Williams-Ellis, with an introduction by Hugh Elles, commander of the Tank Corps, was copyrighted in 1919 and published in New York by Doran. A portrait of Elles after Orpen fronts the book. A contents list runs from a brief account of the tank, its crew, and its tactics at the Armistice, through the earliest tanks and the first battles.

Chapters follow the corps in embryo, then Morval, Flers, and Beaumont-Hamel. Arras, Bullecourt, Messines, and the third battle of Ypres come in turn. Cambrai gets its own chapter, and new tank types, the depot, and the central workshops another. A dated note from the United Service Club, July 28, 1919, signs the introduction. The book is the corps' own first history, written while the paint was fresh.
63269-ocean-tramps:
Ocean Tramps is a set of tales of tramp ships and their men. Stacpoole wrote it, known for his tale of a blue mere. It came out in London in the year 1924 with a verse at its gate. The verse holds that no charm on earth beats the charm of a ship.

Two lads, Bud and Billy, head the first of the tramp tales. A lost ship, a deal with a plain chief, and pearls fill the run. A tale of a race lost at the post and a case in point stand in the midst. The tale of how Billy went broke and the making of a rich man pair off. Isles, flame trees, and a priest house close the set of tales. Stacpoole writes the sea as a home for the loose and the free.
64048-sargasso-of-lost-starships:
Poul Anderson wrote this science fiction story, printed in Planet Stories in January 1952. Far out in space, the blurb warns, Valduma, queen of the voluptuous half-life, plies her trade: a Lorelei of the black void, luring spacemen to death with her siren call. Basil Donovan is drunk again. He sits near the door of the Golden Planet, boots on the table, clutching a tankard of ale.

His captain's stars and silver leaves of an earl of Ansa are tarnished on his stained shirt. His pale cheeks flush deeper, and his eyes smoulder with an old rage. Across the cobbled street a half-timbered house survives the space bombardment, its roof patched, while a bulldozer clears wreckage next door and a well-dressed Terran bosses Ansan workmen. Anderson builds a fallen world in a page, then sends its drunk captain to sea.
64820-the-vibration-wasps:
Frank Belknap Long wrote a space tale that ran in Comet in January 1941. Enormous, they were, like Jupiter, and unutterably terrifying to Joan, the blurb cries over a picture. I was out in space with Joan for the sixth time, Richard begins. It might as well have been the eighth or tenth, he says, for it went on and on.

Every time he rebelled, Joan would shrug and say she would go it alone then. She had about the worst case of exploritis in medical history, he owns, reckless to test if she could live and grow up where human mutants could not. They head for Ganymede, the largest moon of vast mist wrapped Jupiter. Giant wasps and a girl who loves danger drive the tale.
66278-summer-flowers-of-the-high-alps:
Summer Flowers of the High Alps, by Somerville Hastings, is a field book of mountain blooms shown in colour. Hastings had made the Alpine Plants at Home series before it. The pictures here are reproductions from direct colour photographs by the author. A spiny thistle of the high pastures fronts the volume.

Dent of London and Dutton of New York issued the book. A list of kindred guides stands at the front for the traveller. Bennett’s Flora of the Alps and works by the Schröters are named there. Hulme’s Familiar Swiss Flowers keeps them company on the list. Hastings writes for walkers who meet the flowers on the path. Names in English, French, and German go with the plates. The book joins botany with the joy of the high summer hills.
66527-my-home-in-the-alps:
My Home in the Alps, by Mrs Main, gathers notes on Swiss life. Sampson Low of London issued the book in eighteen ninety two. Main also wrote High Alps in Winter and High Life and Towers of Silence. Much of the matter first ran in the Saint Moritz Post paper.

Main lives in Switzerland and wrote to answer traveller queries sent her way. Climbers will find a thrice told tale, she grants, in her notes. Plain tourists get the small facts of Swiss places and Swiss folk. She hopes the book finds a corner in a traveller portmanteau on tour. The preface is signed from Engadiner Kulm in Switzerland that year.
66854-the-mason-wasps:
The Mason Wasps, by Henri Fabre, was turned into English by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and issued at New York in 1919. The contents open with the eumenes, the potter wasps. The odyneri and the pelopeus follow in that order. The ageniae and the prey of the pelopeus take the fourth chapter.

Aberrations of instinct and the swallow and the sparrow widen the subject. Instinct and discernment get a chapter of philosophy from the watching. The nest building odynerus and insect geometry follow in the list. The common wasp fills two chapters near the end of the book. The translator calls this the second wasp volume of the collected Fabre. Mud architecture by small hands is its lasting wonder.
67110-the-hunting-wasps:
Henri Fabre wrote The Hunting Wasps, in Teixeira de Mattos's translation. Hodder and Stoughton put it out at London, New York, and Toronto. The translator's note is dated at Chelsea in 1916. Fabre's essays on wasps will fill three volumes in all, it says. This is the first of those three volumes on the wasps.

The Mason-Wasps and More Hunting Wasps are to follow it. The first seventeen chapters appeared years ago in another version. They come from the first volume of Fabre's entomological souvenirs. Contents open with the buprestis-hunting cerceris and the great cerceris. A scientific slaughterer follows in the chapter heads of the book. Fabre holds that certain books open horizons undreamed of before. His wasps hunt, sting, and store their prey with surgeon's skill. The volume gives those hunts in his patient, wondering prose.
67242-tales-of-the-clipper-ships:
Tales of the Clipper Ships is a book of sea stories by Fox Smith, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1926. A frontispiece by Phil Smith shows the Maid of Athens, like some lovely but wilful lady fallen among evil companions. The contents list six tales. The Last Voyage of the Maid of Athens takes the first seventy pages. The End of an Argument and Oranges follow.

Seattle Sam Signs On, Paddy Doyle's Boots, and The Unlucky Altisidora complete the set. Two of the tales had appeared in the Blue Peter magazine. The first story opens with a burial. Old Thomas Featherstone was dead, and he was also buried, the narrator says dryly. A knot of women with perambulators outside the cemetery gates judged the funeral a skinny show. Dialogue preserved in the copy gives Mrs Pettefer's view, five minutes too late for the funeral itself.
69065-the-isle-of-dead-ships:
The Isle of Dead Ships is a sea adventure by Crittenden Marriott. Lippincott published it in 1909. Frank McKernan drew the illustrations. Copyrights date to 1908 and 1909. A prologue presents the tale's strange setting as sailors' fact.

The isle is a floating mass of wreckage in the Atlantic. Derelict ships drift together in the Gulf Stream's great swirl. No explorer has set foot there and returned to tell. Sailors speak of it in the night watches. The first chapter shifts to San Juan. A prisoner named Frank Howard comes up a gang-plank in handcuffs. An attorney named Renfrew spots him from the deck. Howard is caught at last, he cries.
70621-oxford-and-the-rhodes-scholarships:
Scholz and Hornbeck wrote this handbook on Oxford and the Rhodes Scholarships, issued by Oxford University Press in 1907. Part one traces the source and purpose of the awards, then prints matter drawn from the sixth and last will of Cecil John Rhodes. It follows the steps that set the system up between 1902 and 1906.

Part two turns to Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar sees it. College rule, teaching, courses, degrees and costs are explained in plain order. Lists of scholars and selection boards, plus sample exam papers from January 1907, close a guide built for hopeful students and their advisers.
72511-the-book-of-hats-and-caps:
Elliott's Book of Hats and Caps is a needlework pattern book for knitted and crochet articles. Elliott was needlework correspondent to the Queen newspaper. The book is dedicated, by permission, to the Lady Marion Alford. Faudel, Phillips and Sons of Newgate Street sold it wholesale; Berlin repositories sold it retail. A long advertisement for the firm's Peacock ice silk fronts the patterns. Filoselles in four hundred shades and knitting silks are listed by color.

Elliott's own introduction follows the advertisement. She presents the book as one of useful knitted and crochet articles, with suggestions on the wools used and the mode of washing them. No wool is so cheap as the best, she warns; inferior wool is false economy, constantly tested. The Peacock qualities had won a certificate at the Sydney International Exhibition in 1879. Half-ounce balls, boxed by the dozen in each shade, were the firm's standard pack.
72847-steam-ships:
Steam-Ships, The Story of Their Development to the Present Day, by Fletcher, was published at London in 1910 by Sidgwick and Jackson, with a hundred and fifty illustrations. A front picture shows the William Fawcett, the first steamship of the Peninsular and Oriental line, built in 1829 at two hundred nine tons, flanked by older warships.

The preface notes that steam had passed sail nine to one in world tonnage, all inside little more than a hundred years. A companion volume told the eight century story of sail. Fletcher gives the steam age its own fast, proud history, aimed at an empire that lived by its ships.
73198-the-three-taps:
Ronald Knox wrote The Three Taps, which he called a detective story without a moral. The tale turns on insurance, a trade Knox treats with comic respect in his opening pages. One company, nicknamed the Indescribable, seems to pay out on every mishap.

The chapters bring in a policy with a strange name, a reluctant detective, and a night at an inn called the Load of Mischief. Bredon and Leyland work the case from different sides. A bishop, a late rector, a barmaid, and a scrap of paper all play parts. Three men give three accounts of it all near the end. Knox mixes puzzle, humor, and sharp talk in equal measure.
73464-sailing-ships:
Chatterton wrote Sailing Ships to tell how sailing vessels grew from the earliest times to his own day. Sidgwick and Jackson printed it in London in 1909, with a hundred and thirty pictures. Chatterton wrote for the general reader, not for shipwrights.

He complains that artists of his day draw old ships badly. A chief librarian, he says, could not find one book to guide a painter on period rigs. The book follows each change in hull, sail, and mast that led to the modern sailing ship. A Latin dedication honors his father, who first turned him to the sea. Yachtsmen and sailors, he hopes, will feel the same pleasure he found in the long pedigree of sail.
75142-merrylips:
Beulah Marie Dix published Merrylips in 1906, and Macmillan reissued it for decades; this copy is the 1927 reissue. The dedication explains the heroine at once: the story is for every little girl who has wished for an hour to be a little boy. Merrylips is a maid of the old days, in the England of the civil wars.

Her birthday sends her out into the world, to Larkland and the golden gorse. A tart that was never baked and a silver ring give way to alarums: she becomes a prisoner of war, borrows plumes, and goes off to the wars herself. Brother officers, tidings at Monksfield, and a darkest day follow. Frank Merrill illustrated the book, and Anne Cooper added decorations for the new edition.
75318-the-duke-of-york-s-steps:
Henry Wade published a crime novel in 1929, built around London bankers and a finance firm. Early chapters bring Sir Garth Fratten and his guest Leo Hessel together over wine and old school talk. The contents list points to the Victory Finance Company, an inquest, and a figure named Inez. Inspector John Poole enters partway through the book.

Later chapters turn on papers, alibis, a mine, and a hotel called the Antwerp. Wade lets the case grow out of money dealings rather than a lone act of force. Readers who like calm, step by step inquiry in a period setting will find that pace here.
75553-among-the-camps:
Thomas Nelson Page, the Virginia writer famous for In Ole Virginia, published Among the Camps in 1891 as young people's stories of the war. A front picture freezes a boy's adventure: halt, and bang go the guns in his very face. Page's Two Little Confederates, advertised inside, worked the same ground.

Page wrote the Civil War for children from the southern side: camps, raids, and loyal servants, in dialect and in moonlight. His stories taught a generation of white southern children the Lost Cause as bedtime reading. Modern readers meet the book as a document of how memory was manufactured. Page's craft is real, the tales move, and their charm and their poison arrive in the same sentences.
77092-she-who-sleeps:
Sax Rohmer, creator of Fu Manchu, wrote She Who Sleeps in 1928 and called it a romance of New York and the Nile. The book first ran as a serial in Liberty magazine. Rohmer filled it with Egypt, his favorite ground for mystery.

Lightning opens the tale, and Barry finds himself haunted. The action moves from New York to Cairo and Luxor, then to a camp of excavators in a haunted valley. A lotus sarcophagus, a ritual, and an awakening wait in the middle chapters. A princess, a hieroglyphic letter, and the great Ahmes crowd the close. Rohmer mixes archaeology, love, and the occult at his usual breathless pace.
77199-overcoming-handicaps:
Archer Wallace wrote Overcoming Handicaps, held in 1927 and issued at Garden City, New York, in 1929 by Doubleday, Doran. Wallace had writ Stories of Grit and Canadian Heroes of Mission Fields Overseas. Frank Langford wrote the introduction. Fifteen chapters tell of folk who beat great bar in life.

The Little Cripple with the Giant Mind leads the set. The tale of Arthur Kavanagh and of a delicate boy who became England's greatest sculptor follow. Brave Tusitala, the teller of stories, is Robert Louis Stevenson in his Samoan name. A composer who could not hear his own music is Beethoven in plain terms. A bookbinder's errand boy who became a great scientist and a newsboy who became a great inventor fill the middle. Chapter One opens with Charles Steinmetz, born at Breslau in 1865, a cripple from birth.
78578-the-load-of-chips:
Harriette Newell Woods Baker wrote The Load of Chips under the mark H N W B. Andrew F Graves issued the tale at Boston, entered in eighteen seventy. The Load of Chips stands third in the Sun Shine Series of tales. Honeysuckle Cottage and The Little Florentine fill the first two parts.

Joseph Hickie begs a sixpence at Mrs Irvington’s door at the start. Daddy dead, mammy blind, and all starved, the small boy whines. The lady marks his sound, fed look and practiced begging tone. Work, not coin, is her offer: breakfast in an hour, a shilling by night. Learning to Work and Idleness and Want name its twin moral poles. A broken leg, a jail stay, and a counterfeit bill darken the road. Ten Thousand Dollars and Willie’s Confession close the children’s story.
8801-drum-taps:
Walt Whitman gathers his Civil War poems in Drum-Taps, opening with songs for a prelude, eighteen sixty-one, and the famous call, beat, beat, drums. From Paumanok starting I fly like a bird, Song of the Banner at Daybreak. Rise O Days from your fathomless deeps, Virginia the West, City of Ships, and The Centenarian's Story follow. Cavalry crossing a ford, bivouac on a mountainside, an army corps on the march, and by the bivouac's fitful flame bring the war's camps and marches close.

Come up from the fields father, Vigil strange I kept on the field one night, A march in the ranks hard-pressed. The Wound-Dresser show Whitman's other war: nursing, mourning, and endurance. The poems were written as the war happened, by a poet who visited hospitals and knew its cost.
9490-quaint-courtships:
Quaint Courtships, a Harper's collection from 1906, gathers short love tales by a roster of noted American writers. William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited the set. Names inside include Margaret Deland, Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, and Norman Duncan. Each tale turns on courtship, in its odd, shy, or comic forms.

Deland opens with an encore tale of Old Chester, where a staid captain of seventy finds romance late in life. Other tales move from a harbor town to city rooms, each with its own wooing snag. The tone stays light and fond, with old-style manners throughout. A reader gets a charming sampler of early 1900s American short fiction, all on love's crooked path.
9873-till-the-clock-stops:
J. J. Bell's 1917 novel opens in a London City boardroom, where a young man signs a plain-looking deed for the Aasvogel Syndicate. The deed is filed away and forgotten, but in due season it bears a weighty crop of complex and extraordinary consequences.

Bell, known for his Scottish humor in Wee Macgreegor, here turns to a London tale of business, chance, and fate. The story follows how one quiet act ripples outward into trouble and surprise for everyone touched by it. Readers get a well-made popular novel about small causes and large results.
britannica-1911-agriculture-the-produce-:
The Produce of British Crops forms a statistical section of the Agriculture article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Acreage and livestock returns had been gathered yearly since 1866, but crop produce estimates began only in 1885. The Board of Agriculture appointed local estimators, who reported each autumn on production in their own districts.

Dividing total production by returned acreage gave the average yield per acre for each county. The section warns plainly that these figures are estimates, not exact counts. Much wheat was still in the stack when the numbers appeared. Long tables then give yields across the years for the main British crops, letting readers compare good seasons with poor ones county by county and crop by crop.
britannica-1911-agriculture-the-rotation:
The Rotation of Crops, within the Agriculture article of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, explains why farmers change what each field grows. One crop repeated year after year exhausts the soil for that kind. The plants that follow grow weaker and catch disease more easily. So roots and leguminous crops, the pulse family, are made to follow cereals in a planned order.

Crops grown in rotation also yield more for sale than the same crops grown without a break. Alternated crops gather more mineral matter and nitrogen than cereals do. Most of that richness stays on the farm through manure, while the rest leaves as meat and milk. Cereals sold off the farm are classed as exhaustive, and the crops that restore the soil as restorative.
britannica-1911-alps:
Alps is the joint name for a great mountain system of Europe. Its range entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The chain stretches from south eastern France to the borders of Hungary. It stands between the plains of northern Italy and southern Germany.

The entry calls the Alps the chief land feature of the continent. Unlike the Himalayas or Andes, the chain is not one solid wall. Many ranges split by deep valleys make up the whole mass here. Most valleys run west to east or south west to north east. Deep cross valleys cut the ridges and ease passage through the chain.
britannica-1911-cheops:
Cheops is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the king who, in Herodotus, built the Great Pyramid in Egypt. Herodotus says that Cheops closed the temples, stopped the sacrifices, and made all Egyptians labour on his monument. They worked in relays of 100,000 men, changed every three months. He reigned 50 years. His brother Chephren followed with a reign of 56 years and the second pyramid. The Egyptians suffered every kind of misery under both, the entry reports.

The entry then corrects the tale. Cheops, Chephren, and Mycerinus are real kings of the fourth dynasty, in the right order, and they built the pyramids named for them. But Herodotus places them wholly wrong in time. Manetho puts the pyramid kings correctly in Dynasty IV. In Egyptian the name of Cheops is written Hwfw, Khufu. The Greeks avoided naming these kings, Herodotus says, and called the pyramids after a shepherd, Philition.
britannica-1911-confirmation-of-bishops:
Confirmation of bishops is the act in canon law by which the choice of a new bishop gains assent. That assent must come from the right church authority. In the early church the metropolitan and his bishops, met in synod, confirmed the choice of a suffragan. The fourth canon of the first council of Nicaea set that rule in the year 325.

For a metropolitan no papal assent was needed at first, in West or East. A fresh custom changed that state by slow steps. From the 500s popes gave the pallium to new metropolitans, at first as an honour. That gift came in time to stand for leave to use metropolitan power. By the 800s and 900s Rome pressed that right with force. Yet cases of metropolitans acting without it run into the 1200s. The long entry traces the English form in detail.
britannica-1911-guards-and-household-tro:
Guards and household troops guard a sovereign's person. The practice of keeping bodyguards is very ancient. It may mark the beginning of organised armies. Famous early corps include Xerxes' Immortals and the Mamelukes. Janissaries and Anglo-Saxon huscarles also served that role. Modern usage splits the function in two. Household troops are personal retainers of the sovereign. Guards are an elite corps of fighting men.

The British corps get the fullest treatment. The Yeomen of the Guard date from Henry VII. The Gentlemen-at-Arms began under Henry VIII in 1509. They kept a noble character for centuries. In 1862 they were rebuilt on a purely military basis. Only decorated regular officers could then join. Foreign guards are surveyed as well. The German Guard, in war, fights as a complete army corps.
britannica-1911-hornby-sir-geoffrey-thom:
Geoffrey Thomas Phipps Hornby is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British admiral born in eighteen twenty five. His father was an admiral too, kin to a great earl. The boy went to sea at age twelve in a flagship.

The entry tells how he saw a port town taken in his teens and rose step by step. Party strife left him ashore for years with no ship to command. He ran his father estates in Sussex in that lean time. A call to China at last put him back in charge at sea. There he held a calm hand in a hot row with the United States.
britannica-1911-kay-shuttleworth-sir-jam:
Sir James Phillips Kay Shuttleworth (1804–1877) was an English politician and education reformer, born at Rochdale in Lancashire on the 20th of July 1804, the son of Robert Kay. He first worked in a Rochdale bank, then in 1824 became a medical student at Edinburgh. Settling in Manchester about 1827, he worked for a dispensary in Ancoats and Ardwick.

What he saw of the poor in the factory districts won him in 1835 the post of poor law commissioner. He served first for Norfolk and Suffolk, and later for the London districts. In 1839 he became first secretary of the Privy Council committee for the state education grant. He is remembered for founding at Battersea, with E. Carleton Tufnell, the first training college for school teachers, in 1839 and 1840. The national school system of later days, with its state inspection, grows from that start.
britannica-1911-man-traps: Man-Traps is a brief article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about mechanical devices set to catch poachers and trespassers on private land. The traps took many forms. The most common kind worked like a large rat trap: strong steel springs drove toothed jaws that met in the leg of the victim. The article records the legal end of the practice: since 1827 man-traps have been against the law in England, save inside houses between sunset and sunrise as a defence against burglars.
britannica-1911-mumps:
Mumps is a health entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a catching illness marked by swelling of the spit glands. The ill most often strikes the young and spreads in waves through groups. Its name comes from an old word for a sulk, from the look it gives.

The entry traces the course of the ill from its first cold like signs. Swelling starts by the ear and spreads down to the jaw and neck. The far side of the face may swell in its turn soon after. Pain stays mild, and the parts do not fester or burst. Chewing and swallowing grow hard while the swell lasts, then ease in days.
britannica-1911-salvage-corps:
Salvage Corps is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a London fire service body. The London Salvage Corps is kept up by the fire offices of London. The corps was first formed in the year 1865. It began operations in March of 1866. Its staff at the start numbered sixty four men. Since then the corps has grown much stronger. Its staff now numbers over one hundred men.

It also came from a plain rise in work to do. The stations of the corps are well placed across the city. London has been mapped out into districts for the work. That mapping lets crews reach a fire at the earliest moment. Headquarters sit at Watling Street as the first station. That station guards the City of London itself. A second station stands at Commercial Road. It covers the east and north east of the city.
britannica-1911-shell-heaps:
Shell-heaps is the subject of a past entry in the 1911 Britannica. Shell heaps are mounds of waste from old times. They are found in all parts of the globe. They consist chiefly of shells of sea foods eaten. Bits of beast bone and tools lie mixed in them. Some heaps can still be seen in the making. Heaps on the east coast of Denmark were much studied.

Those heaps were first thought to be raised beaches of old. A close look proved that hands had built them up. Study placed them in a very early age of stone. Tools of polished flint were known at that time. Bones in the heaps show what folk ate then. Wild bull, beaver, seal, and auk bones were found. Large oyster shells gave a clue to lost sea links. The sea near those shores was saltier in that age.
britannica-1911-ward-elizabeth-stuart-ph:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward, an American author and worker for good causes who lived from 1844 to 1911, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Boston, she was the granddaughter of Moses Stuart and the daughter of Austin Phelps, a professor at Andover, and of a mother who also wrote books. The family moved to Andover in 1848.

As a girl she wrote tales for youth magazines and for the Atlantic and Harper's. She wrote many books for the young, above all Sunday school books in series. Her tale The Tenth of January told of a cotton mill that fell and burned at Lawrence in 1860. Her first novel, The Gates Ajar, came in 1868. That study of life after death was widely read and turned into more than one European tongue. More books on the same theme followed across the years.
britannica-1911-zosterops:
Zosterops is a bird entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a wide group of small birds of the old world tropics. The name was first set for one bird kind found in Australia. That first kind proved to be a bird known by two prior names.

The entry says most kinds wear plain mouse hues or soft green on top. White or bright gold at the throat and breast marks some kinds. Bay flanks grace a few kinds in the wide group as well. Most kinds live on one small isle and are found no place else. Some isles hold two kinds, one brown and one green in tone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphe-decha:
Adolphe Dechamps, Belgian statesman and publicist and brother of Cardinal Dechamps, was born at Melle near Ghent on 17 June 1807 and died at Manage on 19 July 1875. His public life began about 1830, soon growing popular through brilliant contributions to Catholic newspapers. With his friend de Decker he founded La Revue de Bruxelles, advocating a system called government of the centres.

Under that scheme, ministries would mix Catholics and Liberals, backed by the moderate elements of both parties. The plan worked successfully for some years, though Dechamps saw that Catholics and Liberals must sooner or later part unless Catholics surrendered their principles. Elected to the Chamber of Representatives in 1834, he won prominence as orator and practical statesman. He debated communal organization in 1836, opposed the Dutch treaty in 1839, and wrote on parties, schools, and Bismarck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-ear:
Six bishops named Alexander are sketched. Alexander of Antioch, thirty-eighth bishop of that see from 413 to 421, earns Theodoret's praise for a holy and austere life. Alexander of Apamea, a Syrian bishop at Ephesus in 431, numbered among eight bishops John's party sent to Emperor Theodosius.
